preamble: Each domain question draws from the complete medical record. Points reflect diagnostic weight. Cost:  Small = existing record / clinical exam / standard labs  |  Medium = targeted lab panel or echo ($200-$1,500)  |  Large = advanced imaging or cath ($1,500-$5,000+)  |  Note: Kawasaki is a CLINICAL diagnosis - no single test confirms it. Signal is distributed across fever, exam findings, and labs.

questions.question: Is there a documented fever >=38.0 C (100.4 F) lasting >=5 days that is unresponsive to antibiotics?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - fever >=5 days is the required anchor criterion for classic Kawasaki diagnosis; antibiotic non-responsiveness rules out bacterial infection

questions.question: In incomplete Kawasaki, is there fever >=5 days with only 2-3 classic features but elevated CRP/ESR and supportive echocardiographic or laboratory findings?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - incomplete Kawasaki accounts for ~20% of cases and is more common in infants <6 months; carries equal coronary aneurysm risk

questions.question: Is there bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection (without discharge or corneal involvement)?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - present in ~90% of classic Kawasaki; bulbar pattern without discharge distinguishes from bacterial/viral conjunctivitis

questions.question: Is there oral mucous membrane changes: strawberry tongue, erythema/cracking of lips, or diffuse oropharyngeal erythema?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - present in ~90% of cases; strawberry tongue is most specific oral finding

questions.question: Is there a polymorphous non-vesicular skin rash (morbilliform, urticarial, or erythema multiforme-like)?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - present in ~80% of cases; perineal accentuation is characteristic and often early

questions.question: Is there peripheral extremity changes: erythema or edema of hands and feet (acute phase) or periungual desquamation (convalescent phase, days 10-21)?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - periungual peeling in convalescent phase is highly characteristic; acute edema/erythema in first week

questions.question: Is there unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy >=1.5 cm, typically anterior cervical?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - least common classic feature (~50-75%); often the presenting complaint prompting evaluation

questions.question: Are there coronary artery aneurysms or dilation on echocardiography (Z-score >=2.5 in LAD or RCA, or absolute diameter >4 mm)?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - coronary involvement confirms diagnosis; Z-score >=2.5 = dilation, >=10 = giant aneurysm with highest thrombosis risk

questions.question: Is there perivascular coronary brightness or lack of tapering of coronary arteries on echo (early or incomplete Kawasaki sign)?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - perivascular brightness may precede measurable dilation; Z-score >=2.0 is supportive in incomplete Kawasaki

questions.question: Is there pericardial effusion, mitral regurgitation, or reduced LV systolic function on echo during acute phase?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - myocarditis and pericarditis occur in ~25-50% of Kawasaki; MR from papillary muscle inflammation

questions.question: Is the ESR >=40 mm/hr and/or CRP >=3.0 mg/dL during the acute febrile phase?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - markedly elevated inflammatory markers are present in virtually all active Kawasaki; ESR/CRP are required supportive criteria in incomplete Kawasaki algorithm

questions.question: Is there leukocytosis (WBC >=15,000/mm3) with neutrophil predominance on CBC during acute phase?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - neutrophilic leukocytosis reflects systemic vasculitic inflammation

questions.question: Is there thrombocytosis (platelets >=450,000/mm3) in the subacute phase (days 7-21)?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - thrombocytosis peaks at 2-3 weeks and correlates with coronary aneurysm risk; giant thrombocytosis (>1M) is a high-risk marker

questions.question: Is there sterile pyuria (>=10 WBC/hpf on urinalysis) or mildly elevated ALT on metabolic panel?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - sterile pyuria in ~80% of Kawasaki; urethral inflammation not UTI; elevated ALT in ~40%; both support diagnosis in incomplete cases

questions.question: Is the patient aged 6 months to 5 years? (Peak incidence 1-2 years; rare under 3 months and over 8 years)
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - 85% of Kawasaki occurs under age 5; very young infants (<6 months) have highest aneurysm risk and most atypical presentations

questions.question: Is the patient of East Asian ancestry (Japanese, Korean, Chinese)? (Incidence 10-30x higher than in Caucasian children)
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - highest absolute risk population; also higher risk of giant aneurysms and IVIG resistance

questions.question: Does the presentation occur in winter or spring months? (Seasonal clustering suggests infectious or environmental trigger)
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - seasonal peak January-March in Northern Hemisphere

questions.question: Was there defervescence (fever resolution) within 36-48 hours of high-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) administration?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - prompt IVIG response is strongly supportive of Kawasaki; ~80% respond to first dose; non-response (IVIG resistance) is itself a high-risk marker

questions.question: Was IVIG administered within the first 10 days of fever, and did repeat echo at 2 weeks and 6-8 weeks show stable or regressing coronary dimensions?
questions.confirmingAnswer: Yes - coronary outcomes are the measure of treatment success; aneurysm regression within 6-8 weeks occurs in ~50% of small-medium aneurysms

high.label: 🔴  80–100 High confidence
high.action: Kawasaki confirmed or highly probable; administer IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin immediately; obtain baseline echo within 24–48 hours; repeat echo at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks

moderate.label: 🟡  50–79 Moderate confidence
moderate.action: Incomplete Kawasaki likely; apply AHA incomplete Kawasaki algorithm; echocardiography indicated urgently; low threshold for empiric IVIG if echo shows coronary changes

low.label: 🟢  <50 Low confidence
low.action: Kawasaki possible but alternative diagnoses should be actively pursued (viral syndrome, bacterial adenitis, drug reaction, toxic shock, adenovirus, MIS-C); complete inflammatory workup; fever diary; cardiology consultation; do not delay if fever persists
